terms.gloss: it is agreed (between us); we agree on
terms.grammar: impersonal use of conveniō: mihi cum aliquō, or inter aliquōs; with ut and the subjunctive
verb: present subjunctive of fīō, “let it be done”
terms.comment: The reply to a proposal: Eāmus intrō hinc. — Fīat.

terms.gloss: agreed, fine by me; placuit, it was agreed, I decided
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.155: posteā mihi placuit, … ut summōrum ōrātōrum Graecās ōrātiōnēs explicārem

terms.comment: The yes of someone who agrees to do what is asked: Sed properā. — Licet.
Grants a point, often before a “but”.

terms.gloss: I have no objection, as far as I’m concerned it’s allowed
terms.grammar: per with the person who allows it, and licet
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.21: digladientur illī, per mē licet (Lewis & Short s.v. digladior)
Caecil. in Cic. Cael. 37: dīde, dīsice, per mē licet (Lewis & Short s.v. disicio)
Traupman 105: I have no objection, per mē licet
terms.comment: “It is allowed as far as I am concerned”: often with a shrug, “let them, for all I care”.

phrases.latin: Mē ad cēnam vocā. — Pol vērō vocō. — Eāmus intrō hinc. — Fīat.
phrases.english: Invite me to dinner. — I certainly do. — Let’s go in, then. — Agreed.
All right, have it your way.

phrases.latin: Sed properā. — Licet. — Jam hīc fac sit, cēna ut cūrētur. — Licet. — Omnian’ licet? — Licet.
phrases.english: But hurry. — OK. — See it’s here, so that dinner gets cooked. — OK. — Everything OK? — OK.
